title: A geopolitical energy shock can reach workers, firms, households, migration, and remittances through a delayed labor-market transmission chain
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Employment and Social Trends: May 2026 Update: Growing labour market risks from the Middle East crisis
geography: Global labor markets with focused exposure analysis for Arab States and Asia and the Pacific, including energy, supply chains, tourism, migration, and remittance channels

denominator.unit: global labor market simulation under oil prices approximately 50 percent above the January-February 2026 average

hours_worked_change_2026.unit: percent projected change in global hours worked in 2026

hours_worked_change_2027.unit: percent projected change in global hours worked in 2027

full_time_equivalent_jobs_2026.unit: full-time-equivalent jobs equivalent to projected 2026 hours decline, approximately

full_time_equivalent_jobs_2027.unit: full-time-equivalent jobs equivalent to projected 2027 hours decline, approximately

real_labour_income_change.unit: percent projected global real labour-income change

observations.method: ILO econometric simulation tracing an illustrative oil-price shock through energy prices, production and transport costs, demand, hours, real labor income, and unemployment.
observations.uncertainty: This is a scenario, not a forecast of the eventual crisis path; results depend on oil-price size, persistence, conflict evolution, substitution, policy response, and model assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Workers, enterprises, households, energy-intensive sectors, informal workers, migrant workers, small firms, and economies exposed to energy and trade routes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Energy substitution, fiscal support, social protection, employment retention, and rapid de-escalation could reduce the modeled labor shock; a price increase may affect sectors differently.

denominator.unit: Arab States labor market scenario frame

hours_rapid_deescalation.unit: percent projected change in hours worked under rapid de-escalation

hours_protracted_conflict.unit: percent projected change in hours worked under protracted conflict

hours_severe_escalation.unit: percent projected change in hours worked under severe escalation

high_exposure_employment.unit: percent of employment in high-exposure sectors including trade, construction, manufacturing, agriculture, transport, and accommodation/food services

migrant_adjustment.value: migrant workers expected to bear a disproportionate share of labor-market adjustment

observations.method: ILO regional modeling and sectoral exposure analysis under rapid de-escalation, protracted-conflict, and severe-escalation scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario ranges are not observed outcomes; sector classifications, labor-market informality, displacement, policy support, and conflict duration affect realized impacts.
observations.subgroup: Arab States workers, migrant workers, refugees, construction and hospitality workers, energy-linked firms, informal workers, and households exposed to conflict and price shocks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Labor-market supports, reconstruction, public employment, social protection, and de-escalation may spread or cushion impacts, while some sectors could recover faster than the aggregate.

observations.period: 2026-2027; Asia and the Pacific spillover through energy, trade, and tourism

denominator.unit: Asia and the Pacific labor-market exposure scenario frame

hours_worked_change_2026.unit: percent projected change in regional hours worked in 2026

hours_worked_change_2027.unit: percent projected change in regional hours worked in 2027

real_labour_income_change.unit: percent projected change in regional real labour income

high_exposure_workers.unit: percent of workers in high-exposure sectors including agriculture, transport, manufacturing, construction, and tourism

transmission_channels.value: imported energy, Gulf-linked labor migration, transport/logistics, tourism, supply chains, and remittances

observations.method: ILO regional scenario modeling and sectoral analysis of energy-import, labor-migration, tourism, trade, and remittance linkages.
observations.uncertainty: The regional projections depend on oil prices, supply-chain duration, exchange rates, labor mobility, tourism recovery, and domestic policy responses; they do not identify country-specific realized losses.
observations.subgroup: Workers and enterprises in Asia and the Pacific, tourism-dependent economies, migrant workers, remittance-receiving households, agricultural and manufacturing workers, and small businesses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Diversified energy sources, domestic demand, alternative migration routes, fiscal support, and remittance resilience could reduce the spillover relative to the scenario.

observations.period: 2026; migrant employment, remittance, and household transmission

denominator.unit: Gulf-linked migrant labor and remittance transmission frame

non_national_employment_sensitivity.unit: percent employment decline among non-nationals associated with each 1 percent decline among nationals in GCC crisis estimates

migrant_outflows.value: exceptionally sharp declines in migrant-worker outflows to GCC countries

remittance_pressure.value: early signs of downward pressure or contraction in remittance flows

household_pathway.value: employment and deployment disruption can reach consumption, poverty, and local employment in origin economies

observations.method: ILO synthesis of crisis-linked migration, non-national employment, repatriation, and remittance channels using available labor-market and macroeconomic evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Early remittance and deployment signals are not a complete measure of household receipt, spending, poverty, or local employment; the relative-sensitivity estimate is context-specific.
observations.subgroup: Migrant workers, non-national workers, labor-sending economies, remittance-receiving households, local firms, refugees, and migrant-worker protection systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Remittances can remain resilient through savings, alternative corridors, exchange-rate changes, family adaptation, or rapid re-employment, while repatriation can reduce risk for some workers.

related_sources.claim: ILO DOI for the May 2026 Employment and Social Trends update.
ILO news summary with global, regional, migrant-worker, remittance, and policy-response implications.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical-shock-to-labor-to-household-transmission route linking energy prices, transport, supply chains, tourism, investment, work hours, labor income, unemployment, migration, remittances, and social protection. It is not individual worker or household respondent data, a realized loss estimate, a completed crisis forecast, or proof that the modeled scenario occurred.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO May 2026 update page, PDF brief, and news summary were reviewed; global oil-shock scenario, Arab States and Asia-Pacific exposure, sector shares, migrant-worker adjustment, remittance channels, and policy-response boundaries were cross-checked.
